list_entry.title: While grapefruit juice is a healthy

A.explanation:
This plan to do low dose + grapefruit juice probably won't work, because .... the variable rate of the supercharging chemical will make it too hard to dose properly.

If one day you take your heart medicine + 6 oz of grapefruit juice and there happens to be 10mg of the medicine-boosting chemical, that will give you a very different medicinal effect then if the following day you take your heart medicine + 6 oz of grapefruit juice and there happens to be 20mg of the chemical.

That extra chemical concentration could create dangerous dosing (if there's too much of the chemical) or ineffective dosing (if there's too little of the chemical).

B.explanation: The fact that the grapefruit juice is cheaper than the medicine almost has no effect, but if anything it would make this plan seem more feasible.

C.explanation:
This answer if anything strengthens the idea that the chemical is the causal difference-maker. When we remove it, the augmenting effect disappears.

But this was never in doubt. This was part of the background evidence that we're already accepting.

D.explanation:
This just tells us how it is that the chemical in grapefruit juice augments medicinal strength. We don't really care about the specifics of how it does it.

We only care about whether it seems wise to adopt a policy of pairing lower doses with a side of grapefruit juice.

E.explanation:
The past status of what doctors used to say isn't really relevant to our current understanding about this chemical and the current plan under consideration.

Until we discovered the chemical in grapefruit juice that was messing up medications, doctors probably had anecdotes about grapefruit juice messing things up and didn't know why but warned their patients to stay away from it.

But now that we understand the chemical, this answer wouldn't really be relevant any more.
